transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi... yeah. Well, to be perfectly honest, I guess I'm really only here because the regular doctor over at the clinic completely got on my case about my eating. I had to go in recently, and she just wouldn't let it go, asking all these questions. But honestly, I think she's making a huge deal out of nothing because she just doesn't understand my schedule or how my life actually works right now. 

I do painting and paperhanging for a living, which is incredibly hands-on, you know? You're up and down ladders all day, matching patterns, constantly moving, driving from one residential site to another, dealing with clients. And on top of that, I'm taking some college classes right now to finish up some credits, which is a whole other level of stress. So most days, I just keep things really, really simple. I'll have my coffee in the morning—I absolutely have to have my coffee just to get out the door and deal with the morning traffic—and then during the day, maybe I'll have a few bites of something quick while I'm sitting in my truck between jobs. Just whatever is easy and doesn't slow me down. And then by the time I finally get home, if I'm not totally swamped with class paperwork or studying for an exam, I might have a small dinner. But if I have a ton of reading or assignments due, I just don't have the time or the energy to sit around cooking some massive meal, you know? I'm just incredibly busy and focused, but she insisted I come talk to you about it, so... here I am.
Do you find yourself wanting to eat when you do have the time?

Well, it's not really about *wanting* to eat, I guess... it's more like, even when I do have a spare hour, which is rare enough as it is between the driving and the prep work and the actual painting, my body just isn't asking for it. Like last weekend, I actually had a Sunday where I didn't have to be on a ladder or reading a textbook, and I was just sitting in my apartment. I had all the time in the world, relatively speaking. And I walked into the kitchen, looked at the fridge, and just... nothing. I didn't feel that pull, you know? It's like my stomach has just gotten used to my schedule, which honestly makes sense if you think about it. If you train your body to run on coffee and momentum, it stops expecting you to stop and eat. Plus, when I do have downtime, my mind is usually still racing. I'm thinking about whether I got the edge perfectly straight on Mrs. Gable's living room wall, or if I need to re-read chapter four for my sociology class, or if I remembered to wash out my good brushes. So sitting down and eating just feels like this... interruption. Even if I have the time, I just don't have the desire to switch gears and focus on food. It just doesn't feel necessary.
Have you lost any weight recently?

Well, I mean, I guess I have lost some, but it's really hard to put a number on it because I don't exactly have time to be weighing myself every morning, you know? But I have noticed it with my work clothes. Like, my favorite pair of painter's pants—the ones with the reinforced knees that I wear all the time because they hold all my tools perfectly—they're just hanging off me lately. I have to pull my belt way tighter than I used to, to the point where it sort of bunches up the fabric in the back, which is super annoying when you're wearing a tool belt over it. And it's not just the clothes, either. The guys I work with, the contractors and the other tradesmen on the job sites, they've been making comments. Like, just last week, this electrician I see on a lot of jobs was like, "Whoa, you're looking a little too thin there, you need to eat a sandwich," which I just find so incredibly condescending, honestly. People think they can just comment on your body when you're a woman on a job site. But anyway, they say I look too thin, but I don't really see it that way at all. To me, it just looks like I've leaned out. When you're climbing up and down ladders for eight hours a day, carrying heavy buckets of paste and rolls of wallpaper, and just constantly staying on your feet, your body is going to change. It's just muscle tone and getting rid of the excess, you know? It's efficiency. So yeah, the pants are loose and people are talking, but I just think my body is finally reflecting how hard I work.
Do you think you would be upset if you started gaining weight again?

Upset? I mean... yeah, honestly, the thought of it really stresses me out. It's not even just about how I look, it's about how I function, you know? Like, if I even think about eating something heavy—say, if someone orders pizza for the crew at a job site, or if I even consider having a big, thick sandwich for lunch—I just get this sudden, overwhelming panicky feeling in my chest. It's like this immediate dread that if I eat that, I'm going to wake up the next day and just feel... bigger. And heavier. And slower. 

And in my line of work, you absolutely cannot be slow or heavy. I have to be light on my feet. I'm constantly shifting my weight on these tall extension ladders, reaching into awkward corners to smooth down wallpaper, or crouching low to tape off baseboards. It takes a lot of agility, and if I put on weight, I just know it would throw off my whole center of gravity. I wouldn't be able to move around the rooms or climb the ladders the way I need to. I'd feel sluggish, and I can't afford to be sluggish when I have deadlines and clients expecting perfection. So yeah, the idea of gaining weight back... it just makes me feel totally out of control, like I'd be losing this edge, this efficiency that I've built up. I just can't let that happen. It would ruin everything about how I manage my day and my work.
Do you think your weight or body shape affects how attractive you feel?

I mean, attractive? I don't really know if "attractive" is the word I'd use, because honestly, who has time to worry about being attractive when you're covered in primer and drywall dust for ten hours a day? But... I guess, yeah, it does affect how I feel about myself. It's more about feeling... clean, I suppose? Like, when I'm lighter, when I don't have all that extra weight dragging me down, I just feel sharper. I feel more put together. 

Like, if I were to gain weight, I think I'd just feel sloppy. And I hate feeling sloppy. In my job, everything has to be so precise. You know, you can't have a sloppy seam on a piece of high-end silk wallpaper—the client will notice immediately, and it ruins the whole room. And I feel like my body is kind of the same way. If it's not lean and tight and efficient, it's just... messy. And if I feel messy, I don't feel good about myself. So I wouldn't say I look in the mirror and think, "Oh, I'm so attractive because I'm thin," it's more like, "I'm acceptable because I'm not taking up unnecessary space." It's just about feeling like I'm in control of my physical form, the same way I'm in control of my brushstrokes. If I lost that control and got bigger, I'd just feel... I don't know, gross, I guess. Like a version of myself that I wouldn't even want to look at, let alone worry about whether someone else found me attractive.
Do you ever avoid eating certain foods because you're afraid of gaining weight?

Well, I mean... it's not so much that I avoid them just because of the weight, but... okay, yes, I suppose I do. But it's more about how those foods make me feel. Like, I have this whole system now. I just can't do heavy carbs anymore. No bread, no pasta, definitely no pastries. Which is actually really hard because there's this bakery right next to the hardware store where I pick up my supplies every Tuesday and Thursday morning, and they always have these huge, fresh-baked muffins and scones in the window. The smell literally fills the whole parking lot. And the guys on the crew, they'll go in and grab these massive breakfast sandwiches on bagels with bacon and cheese, and they'll just inhale them before we even start the prep work for the day. 

And they'll offer me some, or ask if I want them to grab me a muffin, and I always just say I already ate or I'm not hungry. Because if I were to eat one of those scones... I just know exactly what would happen. It would just sit in my stomach like a brick all day. I'd be up on the scaffolding, trying to reach a tricky corner to smooth out some vinyl paper, and all I'd be able to think about is that heavy, dense dough just turning straight into fat. It's like I can almost feel it attaching to my hips and my thighs instantly. 

So I just stick to things that feel safe. Things that are light and clean. Like, I'll bring celery sticks or maybe a few almonds in a little plastic baggie, and I'll just kind of snack on those if I get dizzy. Or I'll just drink black coffee. Lots of black coffee. It keeps my energy up without making me feel weighed down. And I don't do dairy either, because dairy just feels... thick, you know? It feels coating and heavy. So no milk, no cheese, no butter. If I have to cook at home, which I rarely do because I'm usually too exhausted after work, I'll just steam some spinach or maybe have a few slices of cucumber with some lemon juice. 

It's just easier this way. If I start letting those other foods back in, the breads and the cheeses and the heavy stuff, I just know it's a slippery slope. First it's one muffin, and then the next thing I know, my work pants don't fit anymore, and I'm feeling sluggish on the ladder, and I'm losing my edge. I just can't risk it. The anxiety of even looking at a plate of pasta is just... it's too much. It's not worth the panic it causes me. So yeah, I guess I do avoid a lot of things. Most things, really. But it's just what I have to do to keep everything running smoothly.
Do you think you would still avoid certain foods if you didn't think they would make you gain weight?

I mean, that's... gosh, that's a really hard question to even wrap my head around, because the two things are just so completely tied together for me. Like, I don't even know how to separate the food from the weight anymore. Because, like I was trying to explain earlier, the whole reason I get that massive, overwhelming wave of panic when there's heavy food around—like if someone brings in a couple of large pizzas or, I don't know, a giant meatball sandwich—is entirely because of what I know it'll do to my body. 

If you could somehow magically promise me that eating it wouldn't change my shape... I don't know, maybe I wouldn't avoid it? But see, my brain just instantly fast-forwards. I look at a heavy meal, and I don't see food, I just see myself waking up the next morning feeling bigger. And thicker. And just... slower. 

And that's the terrifying part for me, the slowness. Because if I'm bigger, I can't move around the job site the way I need to. I can't squeeze behind a heavy mahogany vanity to cut in the paint on the baseboards, or balance properly on my ladders. I use these really tall, kind of wobbly extension ladders sometimes, especially when I'm working in these older colonial houses with the massive two-story foyer ceilings, and you just have to be so nimble up there. You have to be incredibly light on your feet. You're holding a heavy tray of paint, you're reaching, you're stretching... if your center of gravity is off even a little bit because you've put on weight, it's actually really dangerous. 

So, if I didn't think I'd gain weight... I guess that specific panic wouldn't be there. Because the panic is completely, one hundred percent about that fear of waking up heavier and losing my agility. If I didn't have that dread hanging over me, that absolute terror of not being able to maneuver around the rooms and the scaffolding... maybe I'd eat a slice of pizza. But in reality, I just can't risk it, because I know how bodies work, and I know it *will* make me gain weight, and I just can't let myself get heavy and slow. I just can't.
Would you say your avoidance of certain foods is mostly because of how they make you feel physically or because of the potential weight gain?

It's the weight gain. Definitely the potential weight gain. I mean, the physical feeling of being full is incredibly uncomfortable, sure, but the real issue, the thing that actually makes my heart start racing and my chest get all tight, is the weight. 

Because it's like... the physical feeling of the food in my stomach is just an immediate warning sign. If I eat something heavy, like a slice of pizza or one of those big sandwiches the guys get from the deli, I don't just sit there and think, "Oh, my stomach is full." I get this intense, completely overwhelming panicky feeling that I'll literally wake up the next morning bigger and slower. It's like I can feel the weight attaching to me in real time. 

And that panic is just... it's all-consuming. Because if I wake up bigger and slower, I won't be able to move around the ladders and the rooms the way I need to. And my job is everything to me, you know? I've spent years building up my reputation. Clients will wait six months just to book me for a dining room. If I'm up there on a 12-foot A-frame ladder, trying to perfectly match the pattern repeat on a three-hundred-dollar roll of botanical print, and my center of gravity is off because I've put on weight from eating heavy meals... I could slip. I could tear the paper. I could completely ruin the flow of the room. 

So the physical sensation of the food is really just a trigger for the fear of the weight. The weight gain is the enemy. It's the thing that would take away my agility and my precision. So yeah, it's absolutely the weight gain that I'm avoiding. I just can't let myself get to a point where my body gets in the way of my work. It's just not an option for me.
Do you think you would still feel anxious about your body shape if you were at a healthy weight?

I mean... I don't really know how to answer that. I'm honestly not sure. Because I can't even picture what that would look like or feel like anymore. When you say "healthy weight," my brain just automatically translates that to "heavy." And if I'm heavy, I'm anxious. So I guess... I don't know. I honestly don't know if the anxiety about my shape would just magically disappear if someone told me my weight was technically healthy. 

Because, like I was saying before about the ladders and the scaffolding, my whole sense of... of safety, I guess, is completely tied to being small enough to do my job perfectly. Like, there was this one time, maybe five or six years ago, before I started my own business and I was still apprenticing under this master paperhanger named Tom. And back then, I was probably closer to what you'd call a healthy weight, I guess. I was eating normal lunches, going to the diner with the crew. And I remember we were working in this tiny, cramped powder room in this historic brownstone downtown. The kind with the original exposed plumbing that you have to be so, so careful not to bump into. 

And I was trying to smooth out this really delicate grasscloth wallpaper behind the pedestal sink, and I just felt... clumsy. I felt like my hips were in the way, my arms felt thick, I felt like I was constantly brushing up against the fresh paste and risking ruining the entire drop. And grasscloth is incredibly unforgiving, you know? If you get paste on the front of it, it's completely ruined. You have to scrap the whole sheet, and it costs a fortune, and the clients get furious because the dye lots never match up perfectly if you have to order more. 

So I remember just sitting on the floor of that bathroom, feeling my stomach sort of press against the waistband of my painter's pants, and just having this overwhelming sense of dread about my shape. Like my body was an absolute liability. So if I were back at that weight now... I just don't know. I really don't. I can't imagine feeling okay with it. I feel like the anxiety about my shape would still be there, just screaming at me all the time that I'm taking up too much space. Or maybe it wouldn't? Maybe if I was at a healthy weight, my brain would somehow be different and I wouldn't care? I really have no idea. It's just... it's impossible for me to untangle the shape of my body from the work that I do and the space I need to occupy. So, yeah, I just... I don't know what would happen. I can't even wrap my mind around it.
Do you think you would still feel anxious about your appearance if everyone around you, including your clients and coworkers, told you that you look healthy and fine?

I mean... I really don't know. I honestly couldn't tell you if that would fix it or not. 

Because, well, I work around a lot of different people, right? You've got the other tradesmen on the site—the plumbers, the electricians, the general contractors. And they're mostly guys, and they're not exactly the type to sit around analyzing everyone's body image. But sometimes they'll make offhand comments, you know? Like they'll try to offer me half of their sub sandwich and say something like, "Come on, you gotta keep your strength up to haul those five-gallon paint buckets," or they'll tell me I'm looking good, just trying to be friendly. And even when they say things like that, it doesn't really sink in. It just sort of bounces off me. 

And then there are the clients. My clients are usually these very affluent homeowners, the kind who sometimes hover around the doorways while you're trying to work, offering you sparkling water and asking a million questions about the primer. If one of them came up to me while I was up on the scaffolding, carefully trying to match up the seams on a really expensive, delicate silk-blend wallcovering, and they just out of nowhere said, "You look so healthy and fine"... I don't think it would magically turn off the anxiety. 

Because the anxiety isn't really about what *they* see from across the room. It's about what *I* feel. I could have a whole house full of people clapping and telling me I look absolutely perfect and healthy, but if I bend down to pick up my tape measure or my smoothing brush, and my painter's pants feel even a fraction of an inch tighter against my waist... the panic is just instantly there. It's so loud. It completely drowns out whatever anyone else is saying. 

So I want to say yes, I want to say that having everyone tell me I look fine would be this huge relief, but in reality... I just don't know. My brain just doesn't seem to care what other people think about my appearance. It only cares about how I feel in my own skin and the physical space I'm taking up on the job site. So, yeah, I really don't know if their words would matter at all. I kind of doubt it, honestly.
Do you feel like you would lose control over your eating if you started consuming the foods you currently avoid?

Lose control? Like, just start eating everything in sight? No... no, I really don't think so. That's not... that doesn't really sound like me at all. 

I mean, my whole life, my entire business, is built on absolute, meticulous control. You know? Like, when I'm prepping a room, I don't just slop primer on the walls and hope for the best. I measure every single inch. I calculate the drop, the pattern repeat, the exact amount of paste needed so it doesn't seep through the seams of a delicate fabric wallcovering. I have to be completely in control of every single variable, or the whole project falls apart. 

So if I were to actually eat something I normally avoid—say, I don't know, a big bowl of pasta or a heavy pastry from that bakery down the street from my current job site—I wouldn't suddenly just lose my mind and eat five more. It's not like a dam breaking. The problem isn't that I'd lose control of my eating... the problem is just the overwhelming panic about what that *one* pastry or that *one* bowl of pasta is going to do to my body. I'd eat it, and I'd stop, because I'm very disciplined. I've always been incredibly disciplined. But then I'd just be stuck with that heavy, awful feeling in my stomach, and the absolute terror that I'm going to wake up too sluggish to climb the scaffolding tomorrow. 

So, no, it's not about losing control of the food. If anything, I'm almost too controlled, you know? Like, my apprentices always joke that I'm a machine because I never break my routine. We'll be on a massive job, like this huge foyer with 20-foot ceilings we did last month, and they're all ordering massive amounts of takeout and going back for seconds, and I'm just... I'm focused. I know exactly what I'm doing and exactly what my limits are. 

So the idea of just losing control and eating everything... no, I haven't ever felt like that. I don't think that would happen at all. I just don't want the weight from the food in the first place. That's really all it is.
Is there anything else, besides the fear of gaining weight, that contributes to your decision to avoid certain foods?

I mean... let me think about that. Because, no, I really don't think there is. It’s pretty much entirely just... just the weight. And the shape. Like, people ask me all the time if I have allergies or if I'm doing some specific trendy diet, and I always have to figure out how to brush it off. 

Just last week, actually, I was working on this massive dining room—gorgeous space, custom wainscoting on the bottom half, and we were doing this incredibly intricate William Morris botanical print on the top half. It required so much concentration because the pattern repeat was huge and you can't afford to waste a single drop. Anyway, the homeowner, this really sweet lady, she had this massive spread catered for the crew. Like, artisanal sourdough sandwiches, three different kinds of pasta salad, these huge chocolate chunk cookies from that famous bakery downtown. 

And when I politely declined, she got so concerned and started asking if I was celiac, or lactose intolerant, or if I was vegan, because she felt so terrible that she didn't provide accommodations. And I had to stand there, holding my smoothing tool, trying to explain away why I wasn't eating without sounding completely crazy. But the truth is, I don't care about gluten. I don't have any ethical issues with dairy or meat. I don't have a sensitive stomach or anything like that. I'm not avoiding those foods because of how they taste or where they come from or some kind of health condition. 

It always, always just comes back to the weight. It's just that pure, absolute dread of what eating those things will do to my body. Like, if I ate that sourdough sandwich or even just a handful of that pasta salad, all I would be able to think about for the rest of the day—the rest of the week, even—is how that food is making me heavier, how it's making my stomach stick out, how my work pants are going to feel tighter tomorrow morning when I'm bending over to mix the primer. I just picture the number on the scale going up, and it completely paralyzes me. 

So, no, there isn't some other underlying reason. It’s not about digestion or allergies or anything else. It's literally just the terror of gaining weight and taking up more space. That's the only thing that dictates what I will or won't put in my body. I almost wish I could say it was something simpler like a gluten intolerance, because it would make explaining things to clients a whole lot easier, but... yeah. It's just the fear of the weight. Nothing else.
Do you think your weight is the only factor that determines your attractiveness?

I mean... I guess logically, no? Like, if I really stop and force myself to think about it, I know there are other things that make a person attractive. But... I don't know. It’s hard to explain how it actually feels in my head. 

It’s sort of like... okay, think about it in terms of my work, right? When you’re prepping a room, the absolute most important part—the part that dictates everything else—is the foundation. The walls have to be perfectly smooth. If you have uneven drywall, or if someone did a terrible patch job on a hole and didn't sand it down properly, or if there's an old texture that hasn't been completely skim-coated... it completely ruins whatever goes on top. You could be hanging the most exquisite, hand-painted, $500-a-roll imported wallpaper. You could have these gorgeous, expensive sconces highlighting it. But if the wall underneath is lumpy or flawed, that is literally all you are going to see. The whole wall is just ruined. 

And that’s... that’s kind of exactly how I view my own attractiveness. Like, sure, maybe I have nice eyes, or maybe my hair looks okay even when I just have it pulled back under a messy bun or a baseball cap on the job site. My sister is always telling me I have a great smile, and she's always trying to get me to wear nicer clothes when I'm not working, instead of just swimming in my oversized, paint-splattered hoodies. So I know, in theory, that people look at faces and hair and style and all of that. 

But for me, the weight is the drywall. It’s the foundation. If my weight isn't right—if I feel like I'm taking up too much space, or if my stomach isn't perfectly flat, or if my arms look even a tiny bit soft when I'm reaching up to cut in a ceiling—then none of those other things matter at all. The expensive wallpaper doesn't matter if the wall is ruined, you know? The weight just completely overrides everything else. I'll look in the mirror before I leave for a job, maybe I'm just running to the Sherwin-Williams store at 6 AM to pick up some custom tints, and if my work pants feel even slightly snug against my hips, I can't even look at my face. I couldn't tell you if my hair looks nice or if my skin is clear because all I see, all I can possibly focus on, is the shape of my body. 

So... I want to say no, it's not the only factor, because I know that sounds so one-dimensional. It sounds ridiculous to say that absolutely nothing else matters. But in my day-to-day life... it really does feel like it's the only thing that actually counts. If the weight isn't perfectly, strictly controlled, then I just feel completely repulsive, no matter what else I have going for me.
Do you think you would still restrict your food intake if you weren't afraid of gaining weight?

If I wasn't afraid of gaining weight? Um... honestly, no. I really don't think I would restrict at all. Because if you take away that fear... what's left? Like I was saying before, it’s not about disliking food or having a bad stomach. It really is just that one specific, overwhelming fear. 

It’s just... if I eat something heavy, like, say, a couple slices of pizza or one of those really big, thick deli sandwiches that the guys on the crew are always getting for lunch from the corner bodegas... if I even take a few bites of something like that, I immediately get this intense, panicky feeling. It just completely washes over me. I start obsessing over the idea that I'm going to wake up the next morning bigger, and heavier, and just... slower. 

And in my line of work, I absolutely cannot be slow or heavy. My body is basically my most important tool, you know? I'm constantly up and down ladders, moving heavy scaffolding, squeezing into tight corners behind pedestal sinks to get the wallpaper seams perfectly aligned, reaching above my head for hours at a time to cut in the ceiling trim. Like, just yesterday we were doing this intricate crown molding in this old Victorian home, and you have to be so nimble. You're balancing, you're stretching, you're twisting your torso in these weird ways just to get the brush at the exact right angle without dripping on the floor. 

If I wake up feeling bigger and slower because I ate that heavy sandwich, I just feel like I won't be able to move around the ladders and the rooms the way I need to. I'd feel completely off-balance and clumsy, and I'd probably mess up the paint job or, worse, fall off the scaffolding because my center of gravity feels wrong. The panic about that is just so real and so physical. It's like my brain is screaming at me that the food is going to physically weigh me down and ruin my ability to do my job. 

So, yeah, if you could somehow magically take away that fear of getting bigger and gaining the weight... I don't think I'd have any problem eating. I really don't. It's just that right now, I can't separate the food from that absolute panic of what the weight is going to do to my body and my movement.
Is your fear of gaining weight the main reason you restrict what you eat?

Yeah, exactly. I know I'm probably sounding like a broken record here since I basically just said that, but... yes. It is absolutely the main reason. Really, it's the only reason. 

I mean, I just can't emphasize enough how consuming that fear is. Like I was just trying to explain with the guys on the crew and their lunches... if I were to actually sit down and eat something heavy like that pizza or a big sub sandwich, it’s not the food itself I'm running from, it's that immediate, suffocating panic that hits me. I just get this overwhelming dread that I’m going to wake up the very next day literally bigger. Like, physically heavier, puffier, and just... slower. 

And when your whole livelihood depends on your body, that fear just takes over everything. When you're up twenty feet on an extension ladder, or balancing on a narrow plank of scaffolding trying to perfectly align a seam on a wall, you have to be light. You have to be agile. If I have that heavy food in me, my brain just completely convinces me that the weight is already there, and I'll be too big and slow to move around the ladders and the rooms the way I need to. I'll just feel entirely clumsy, like my center of balance is totally thrown off because of the extra weight, and I won't be able to trust my footing. 

So, yeah... I'm sorry, I know I'm rambling and circling back to the exact same point, but it really is just that fear. It's the panic of gaining the weight and what that weight will do to my ability to move. That's the entire reason I restrict.
Is your fear of gaining weight the only reason you restrict your food intake?

I mean... yes. It really is the only reason, not just the main one. I know I'm totally repeating myself here, and I'm sorry, I feel like I'm just talking in circles today, but it’s just the absolute truth. 

Like I was just saying with the pizza and those big sandwiches the crew gets... if I eat something heavy like that, I'm not avoiding it because I don't like the taste, or because I have allergies, or because I'm trying to follow some specific health trend or whatever. It's literally just that panicky feeling. I get this intense, immediate panic that if I eat it, I'll wake up tomorrow bigger and slower. And I just keep picturing myself trying to move around the ladders and the rooms the way I need to, and I just know I wouldn't be able to do it. 

Like, think about when you're painting a two-story foyer or a really tricky stairwell. You have to set up these pivot tools and ladder levelers, and you're constantly shifting your weight, reaching over the banister with an extension pole just to cut in the corners... If I'm heavier, or even if my brain just convinces me I'm heavier and slower because of what I ate, I'd honestly be a danger to myself. I wouldn't be able to maneuver around the room or climb up and down all day carrying heavy gallons of paint and those thick canvas drop cloths. 

So, yeah, I really don't have any other reasons at all. That fear of getting bigger and not being able to move the way I need to for my job... that is one hundred percent the only reason I restrict. There's really nothing else behind it. Just that overwhelming panic about the weight and how it would slow me down.
Do you think your weight is the only thing that determines how you see your body?

Um... no, I really don't think it's just the weight. I mean, the actual number on the scale is a huge part of it, obviously, but it's definitely not the only thing. It’s also just... the shape of my body, you know? The physical space I take up. 

Like, I have these standard white canvas painter's pants that I wear to work every single day. You know the type, they have the reinforced knees and the little loop on the side for a hammer or a putty knife, and all those deep pockets for your utility knife and your tack cloths. Anyway, when I get dressed in the morning at, like, 5:30 AM before I head out to the job site, it's not just about what I might weigh, it's about exactly how those pants feel on my body. If they pull even a fraction of an inch tighter around my thighs or my waist, or if I look in the mirror and my shape just looks... I don't know, wider, or softer, or rounder... it completely dictates how I feel about myself for the rest of the day. 

And then when I'm actually on the job, if I catch my reflection in a window pane while I'm rolling a large wall or kneeling down to tape off a baseboard, and my arms look bulky to me, or my stomach doesn't look perfectly flat under my t-shirt... it's just as bad as if the scale had gone up ten pounds. It’s the dimensions of my body. The shape of it. 

So, no, it's definitely not just the weight itself. It's how my clothes fit, how my shape looks in the mirror, how much physical room I feel like I'm taking up when I'm moving around the room. patient.answer:
I mean... let me think about that. Because, no, I really don't think there is. It’s pretty much entirely just... just the weight. And the shape. Like, people ask me all the time if I have allergies or if I'm doing some specific trendy diet, and I always have to figure out how to brush it off. 

Just last week, actually, I was working on this massive dining room—gorgeous space, custom wainscoting on the bottom half, and we were doing this incredibly intricate William Morris botanical print on the top half. It required so much concentration because the pattern repeat was huge and you can't afford to waste a single drop. Anyway, the homeowner, this really sweet lady, she had this massive spread catered for the crew. Like, artisanal sourdough sandwiches, three different kinds of pasta salad, these huge chocolate chunk cookies from that famous bakery downtown. 

And when I politely declined, she got so concerned and started asking if I was celiac, or lactose intolerant, or if I was vegan, because she felt so terrible that she didn't provide accommodations. And I had to stand there, holding my smoothing tool, trying to explain away why I wasn't eating without sounding completely crazy. But the truth is, I don't care about gluten. I don't have any ethical issues with dairy or meat. I don't have a sensitive stomach or anything like that. I'm not avoiding those foods because of how they taste or where they come from or some kind of health condition. 

It always, always just comes back to the weight. It's just that pure, absolute dread of what eating those things will do to my body. Like, if I ate that sourdough sandwich or even just a handful of that pasta salad, all I would be able to think about for the rest of the day—the rest of the week, even—is how that food is making me heavier, how it's making my stomach stick out, how my work pants are going to feel tighter tomorrow morning when I'm bending over to mix the primer. I just picture the number on the scale going up, and it completely paralyzes me. 

So, no, there isn't some other underlying reason. It’s not about digestion or allergies or anything else. It's literally just the terror of gaining weight and taking up more space. That's the only thing that dictates what I will or won't put in my body. I almost wish I could say it was something simpler like a gluten intolerance, because it would make explaining things to clients a whole lot easier, but... yeah. It's just the fear of the weight. Nothing else.

patient.answer:
I mean... I guess logically, no? Like, if I really stop and force myself to think about it, I know there are other things that make a person attractive. But... I don't know. It’s hard to explain how it actually feels in my head. 

It’s sort of like... okay, think about it in terms of my work, right? When you’re prepping a room, the absolute most important part—the part that dictates everything else—is the foundation. The walls have to be perfectly smooth. If you have uneven drywall, or if someone did a terrible patch job on a hole and didn't sand it down properly, or if there's an old texture that hasn't been completely skim-coated... it completely ruins whatever goes on top. You could be hanging the most exquisite, hand-painted, $500-a-roll imported wallpaper. You could have these gorgeous, expensive sconces highlighting it. But if the wall underneath is lumpy or flawed, that is literally all you are going to see. The whole wall is just ruined. 

And that’s... that’s kind of exactly how I view my own attractiveness. Like, sure, maybe I have nice eyes, or maybe my hair looks okay even when I just have it pulled back under a messy bun or a baseball cap on the job site. My sister is always telling me I have a great smile, and she's always trying to get me to wear nicer clothes when I'm not working, instead of just swimming in my oversized, paint-splattered hoodies. So I know, in theory, that people look at faces and hair and style and all of that. 

But for me, the weight is the drywall. It’s the foundation. If my weight isn't right—if I feel like I'm taking up too much space, or if my stomach isn't perfectly flat, or if my arms look even a tiny bit soft when I'm reaching up to cut in a ceiling—then none of those other things matter at all. The expensive wallpaper doesn't matter if the wall is ruined, you know? The weight just completely overrides everything else. I'll look in the mirror before I leave for a job, maybe I'm just running to the Sherwin-Williams store at 6 AM to pick up some custom tints, and if my work pants feel even slightly snug against my hips, I can't even look at my face. I couldn't tell you if my hair looks nice or if my skin is clear because all I see, all I can possibly focus on, is the shape of my body. 

So... I want to say no, it's not the only factor, because I know that sounds so one-dimensional. It sounds ridiculous to say that absolutely nothing else matters. But in my day-to-day life... it really does feel like it's the only thing that actually counts. If the weight isn't perfectly, strictly controlled, then I just feel completely repulsive, no matter what else I have going for me.

It’s just... if I eat something heavy, like, say, a couple slices of pizza or one of those really big, thick deli sandwiches that the guys on the crew are always getting for lunch from the corner bodegas... if I even take a few bites of something like that, I immediately get this intense, panicky feeling. It just completely washes over me. I start obsessing over the idea that I'm going to wake up the next morning bigger, and heavier, and just... slower. 

And in my line of work, I absolutely cannot be slow or heavy. My body is basically my most important tool, you know? I'm constantly up and down ladders, moving heavy scaffolding, squeezing into tight corners behind pedestal sinks to get the wallpaper seams perfectly aligned, reaching above my head for hours at a time to cut in the ceiling trim. Like, just yesterday we were doing this intricate crown molding in this old Victorian home, and you have to be so nimble. You're balancing, you're stretching, you're twisting your torso in these weird ways just to get the brush at the exact right angle without dripping on the floor. 

If I wake up feeling bigger and slower because I ate that heavy sandwich, I just feel like I won't be able to move around the ladders and the rooms the way I need to. I'd feel completely off-balance and clumsy, and I'd probably mess up the paint job or, worse, fall off the scaffolding because my center of gravity feels wrong. The panic about that is just so real and so physical. It's like my brain is screaming at me that the food is going to physically weigh me down and ruin my ability to do my job. 

So, yeah, if you could somehow magically take away that fear of getting bigger and gaining the weight... I don't think I'd have any problem eating. I really don't. It's just that right now, I can't separate the food from that absolute panic of what the weight is going to do to my body and my movement.
